summary: This document specifies conventions for using NIST's post-quantum signature algorithm ML-DSA (FIPS 204) in X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists. It also covers how signatures and key material are encoded.

plainLanguage.summary: An X.509 certificate carries the name of the algorithm that signed it and the public key to check that signature with. This document adds the names and the encodings for ML-DSA, the signature scheme NIST published to resist quantum computers. It fixes what goes in each field, how large the keys and signatures are, and how a private key may be stored so that it can be moved between systems.

subtitle: How to put NIST's quantum-resistant ML-DSA signatures and keys into X.509 certificates and CRLs.

tldr.problem: Certificates and revocation lists need a way to name the algorithm that signed them and to carry the signer's public key. The existing names cover the algorithms in use today, none of which can resist a future quantum computer.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9881 registers three object identifiers for NIST's ML-DSA signature scheme and gives the exact encodings for it: an algorithm identifier with no parameters, a signature value computed over the DER-encoded certificate, and a raw public key of a fixed size in the subjectPublicKey field. It also defines how a private key may be stored.
tldr.outcome: Certification authorities can issue ML-DSA certificates and clients must recognise the identifiers. The document covers the three security levels ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87, and forbids the HashML-DSA variant so that one key type means one thing across the Internet.

today: RFC 9881 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025, and it has not been obsoleted. IANA has registered the ASN.1 module id-mod-x509-ml-dsa-2025 in the SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier registry with the decimal value 119, and the three algorithm object identifiers come from NIST's Computer Security Objects Register.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm is a quantum-resistant digital signature scheme standardized by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology PQC project in FIPS 204. This document specifies the use of ML-DSA in Public Key Infrastructure X.509 certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists at three security levels: ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87.

FIPS 204 defines two variants of ML-DSA, pure and pre-hash. Only the former is specified in this document, and the rationale is given in Section 8.3. The pure variant of ML-DSA supports the typical pre-hash flow, which is described in Appendix D.

Prior to standardization, ML-DSA was known as Dilithium. ML-DSA and Dilithium are not compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: ML-DSA is the name NIST gave to the signature scheme it standardized to survive attacks by a future quantum computer. This document says how to use it in the certificates and revocation lists that the Internet's public key infrastructure is built from. It covers three sizes of the scheme, chosen for three levels of security. The scheme was previously called Dilithium, and the two names do not describe the same algorithm.

sections.title: Identifiers
sections.content:
The AlgorithmIdentifier type is a SEQUENCE with two fields: an algorithm field that identifies the cryptographic algorithm with an object identifier, and an optional parameters field holding the parameters associated with that algorithm.

The NIST-registered object identifiers are id-ml-dsa-44, id-ml-dsa-65 and id-ml-dsa-87, which expand to the arcs joint-iso-itu-t, country United States, organization Government, csor, nistAlgorithm, sigAlgs, and then the values 17, 18 and 19.

The contents of the parameters component for each algorithm must be absent.
sections.plainLanguage: Every algorithm in a certificate is named by a number called an object identifier. Three identifiers are registered here, one for each security level. Unlike some algorithms, ML-DSA carries no extra parameters alongside the identifier, so the identifier stands alone.

sections.title: Signatures in Certificates and CRLs
sections.content:
ML-DSA is a digital signature scheme built on the Fiat-Shamir-with-aborts framework, and its security is based on the hardness of lattice problems over module lattices. It provides three parameter sets for the NIST PQC security categories 2, 3 and 5.

Signatures are used in a number of ASN.1 structures. In an X.509 certificate, a signature is encoded with an algorithm identifier in the signatureAlgorithm attribute and a signatureValue attribute that holds the actual signature. The same arrangement is used in a Certificate Revocation List, where the signatureAlgorithm and signatureValue attributes appear in the list structure.

The identifiers defined in Section 2 can be used as the AlgorithmIdentifier in the signatureAlgorithm field of the certificate and CRL structures and in the signature field of the structures to be signed. The parameters of these signature algorithms must be absent, so the AlgorithmIdentifier is a SEQUENCE of one component, the object identifier. The signatureValue field contains the corresponding ML-DSA signature computed over the ASN.1 DER-encoded structure to be signed. The optional context string parameter is left at its default value, the empty string.

Conforming certification authority implementations must specify the algorithms explicitly using these object identifiers when encoding ML-DSA signatures in certificates and CRLs, and conforming client implementations that process certificates and CRLs using ML-DSA must recognise the corresponding identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: In a certificate, the signature algorithm is named in one field and the signature itself is stored in another, and the same pattern is used in a revocation list. The signature is computed over the DER-encoded bytes of the part of the certificate that the issuer is signing, which is the part that holds the subject and the issuer's own name. An issuer must name the algorithm explicitly, and a client must know the name.

sections.title: Public Keys in Certificates
sections.content:
In an X.509 certificate the subjectPublicKeyInfo field holds an algorithm identifier and a subjectPublicKey bit string that contains the public key.

Algorithm 22 in Section 7.2 of FIPS 204 defines the raw byte string encoding of an ML-DSA public key. When used in a SubjectPublicKeyInfo type, the subjectPublicKey bit string contains this raw byte string encoding of the public key. When an ML-DSA public key appears outside a SubjectPublicKeyInfo type in an environment that uses ASN.1 encoding, it could be encoded as an OCTET STRING using the types defined below.

The public key types are ML-DSA-44-PublicKey, an OCTET STRING of 1,312 bytes; ML-DSA-65-PublicKey, an OCTET STRING of 1,952 bytes; and ML-DSA-87-PublicKey, an OCTET STRING of 2,592 bytes. Each public key type is tied to its algorithm identifier and to the permitted certificate key usages of digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyCertSign and cRLSign.

The Asymmetric Key Package format of RFC 5958 is used to encode a private key or keypair in a structure that identifies the algorithm and can also hold the public key and additional attributes. Appendix C of the document contains example ML-DSA public keys encoded using the textual encoding of RFC 7468.
sections.plainLanguage: The public key goes into the certificate as a plain byte string, with no wrapping structure around it. The three key sizes are fixed: 1,312 bytes for the smallest security level, 1,952 for the middle and 2,592 for the largest. The document also gives a way to store a private key together with its public key in one structure.

sections.title: Key Usage Bits
sections.content:
The intended application for the key is indicated in the keyUsage certificate extension. If the keyUsage extension is present in a certificate that includes an ML-DSA identifier in the SubjectPublicKeyInfo, then the subject public key can only be used for verifying digital signatures on certificates or CRLs, or those used in an entity authentication service, a data origin authentication service, an integrity service, and a non-repudiation service that protects against the signing entity falsely denying some action.

That means the keyUsage extension must have at least one of the following bits set: digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyCertSign or cRLSign.

ML-DSA subject public keys cannot be used to establish keys or encrypt data, so the keyUsage extension must not have any of the following bits set: keyEncipherment, dataEncipherment, keyAgreement, encipherOnly or decipherOnly. The requirements about the keyUsage extension bits defined in RFC 5280 still apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate can say what its key may be used for. An ML-DSA key signs and does nothing else, so it may be marked for signing, for proving authorship, or for signing certificates and revocation lists, and it must not be marked for encrypting data or agreeing on keys.

sections.title: Private Key Format
sections.content:
FIPS 204 specifies two formats for an ML-DSA private key: a 32-octet seed and an expanded private key. The expanded private key, and the public key, are computed from the seed using the key generation function.

The privateKey field of the OneAsymmetricKey structure of RFC 5958 contains one of three DER-encoded forms. The seed form, tagged [0], holds just the 32-byte seed value from which both the expanded private key and the public key can be derived. The expandedKey form holds the expanded private key that was derived from the seed. The both form holds the seed and the expanded private key together, which allows interoperability between systems that want to keep the seed and systems that only support expanded private keys.

Any of the three forms may be used, though the seed form is recommended for storage efficiency. The privateKeyAlgorithm field uses the AlgorithmIdentifier structure with the appropriate object identifier, and the publicKey field, if present, holds the encoded public key.

While the private key can be stored in several formats, the seed-only form is recommended as the most compact representation, and both the expanded private key and the public key can be derived deterministically from the seed. The publicKey field and the expandedKey form are technically redundant when the seed-only form is used, but they may be included to enable keypair consistency checks during import operations.

When parsing the private key, the ASN.1 tag explicitly indicates which variant is present. Implementations should use the context-specific tag for seed, the OCTET STRING tag for expandedKey and the SEQUENCE tag for both, rather than any heuristic such as the length of the enclosing OCTET STRING.
sections.plainLanguage: A private key can be stored in three ways: as the 32-byte seed it came from, as the full expanded key, or as both. The seed is enough to reconstruct everything else, and the document recommends keeping it because expanding it is a one-way operation. The encoding says which form is in use by its ASN.1 tag, so a reader does not have to guess from the length.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The seed represents the recommended format for storing and transmitting ML-DSA private keys. FIPS 204 explicitly permits it as an acceptable representation of a keypair, and in particular allows a seed generated in one cryptographic module to be imported or exported into another module.

Unlike other private key compression methods, expanding a private key from a seed is a one-way function: once a full key has been expanded from the seed and the seed discarded, the seed cannot be recreated even if the full expanded private key is available. For this reason, it is recommended that implementations retain and export the seed even when also exporting the expanded private key.

When receiving a private key that contains both the seed and the expanded key, the recipient should perform a seed consistency check to ensure that the sender properly generated the private key. The check consists of regenerating the expanded form from the seed and ensuring it is bytewise equal to the value presented. If the check is done and the two do not match, the recipient must reject the private key as malformed. Recipients that do not perform the check avoid key generation and comparison operations but cannot confirm that the seed and the expanded key match.

Section 8.3 explains why the HashML-DSA mode of FIPS 204 must not be used, and why public keys identified by the HashML-DSA identifiers must not appear in X.509 certificates used for CRLs, OCSP, certificate issuance and related PKIX protocols. The restriction is primarily to increase interoperability. ML-DSA and HashML-DSA are incompatible algorithms that need different verification routines, and the same object identifiers are used for ML-DSA public keys and ML-DSA signature algorithms, so an implementation would have to commit a public key to one of the two types at the time the certificate is created. That is expected to cause operational issues where the operator does not know at key-generation time whether the key will need to produce pure or pre-hashed signatures. The External mode described in Appendix D avoids these concerns. A minor security reason is that ML-DSA prepends a hash of the public key to the message before hashing, which gives it enhanced resistance against collision attacks compared with HashML-DSA or conventional RSA or ECDSA signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: Two operational points matter. First, keep the seed: once the full key has been produced from it and the seed thrown away, the seed cannot be recovered, and the seed is the compact form that moves between systems. Second, when a key arrives with both a seed and an expanded form, the two can be checked against each other to catch a key that was not generated properly. The document also rules out a second variant of the algorithm, HashML-DSA, because the two variants need different verification code and share the same identifiers, which would leave an implementer guessing which one a key was for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5280 apply to this specification as well. The ML-DSA signature scheme is strongly unforgeable under chosen message attacks, and for the purpose of estimating security strength it has been assumed that the attacker has access to signatures for no more than 2^64 chosen messages.

ML-DSA depends on high quality random numbers suitable for use in cryptography. Using inadequate pseudo-random number generators to generate such values can significantly undermine various security properties: using an inadequate generator for key generation might allow an attacker to recover the private key by trying a small set of possibilities rather than searching the whole keyspace.

The design of ML-DSA takes care to make side-channel resilience easier to achieve. ML-DSA does not depend on Gaussian sampling. Implementations must still take great care not to leak information through side channels, and while deliberate design decisions help deliver a secure implementation with greater ease, particularly against side-channel attacks, they do not provide resistance to more powerful attacks such as differential power analysis. Some amount of side-channel leakage has been demonstrated in parts of the signing algorithm, specifically the bit-unpacking function, from which a demonstration of key recovery has been made over a large sample of signatures. Masking countermeasures exist for ML-DSA, but come with a performance overhead.

ML-DSA offers both deterministic and randomized signing, and signatures generated with either mode are compatible, so a verifier cannot tell them apart. In the deterministic case a signature depends only on the private key and the message, which makes the implementation easier to test and needs no randomness source during signing. In the randomized case signing mixes in a 256-bit random string from an approved random bit generator, and ML-DSA is easier to harden against fault and hardware side-channel attacks.

ML-DSA possesses three security properties associated with non-repudiation: exclusive ownership, message-bound signatures and non-resignability. These are based tightly on the assumed collision resistance of the hash function used, in this case SHAKE-256.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme needs good random numbers, and it needs them for key generation in particular: a weak generator would let an attacker recover a private key by trying a few values instead of searching the whole space. The design avoids Gaussian sampling, which is a common source of timing leaks, but that does not make implementations automatically safe, and leakage has been shown in the bit-unpacking step of signing. Signing can be deterministic, which is easier to test, or randomized, which is easier to harden against fault attacks.
